chapter: Producing, state of New Orleans music
title: Production company and the Wild Tchoupitoulas
summary: He explains how the company produces acts, from LaBelle to the Wild Tchoupitoulas, without his playing on them.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: But it could happen as well as anyone else. One thing that you all somewhat did together was, didn't you produce the Wild Chopper Tulas album?

The company here, parent company, produced it. I didn't go in with the Wild Chopper Tulas. This being a production company that Marshall and myself own, some of the things that we produce doesn't mean that I go in with it. I'm glad you're explaining that. When we produce LaBelle, I produce LaBelle. Every step of the way, every moment. Some other groups do their own thing enough, whereas I don't do my thing what I do musically with them, but I am still a part of the production company. We produce them. How do you do that? By listening to what they're having, approving it. Even if you don't like it, give it a chance. Sometimes that's the job of a producer.

So, that. So Marshall did the Wild Chopper Tulas album? You might say, yeah. Because that was just, to me, just a thing of beauty as it captures the street sound. Oh, yeah. Right. What made you decide to go record Motion in California? Jerry Wexton.
Right. It was up to the producer to pick places and things, and he did. I was all for it. Whoever's leading them for.

You wanted to put it in someone else's hands? Oh, yes. Lovely. What are your plans for the new album? Would that be produced locally or? Local. Very local. Will you be producing that or Marshall? Myself. I wanted two more general questions. What do you think could... Would you say, and how would you react to this statement, that some of the very strengths of New Orleans music, in that it's loose and enjoyable, or sometimes very downfall, that the musicians aren't business-like enough? that sometimes the fun aspects of being in New Orleans, that give us so much great music, can also be the downfall, in that we don't get the exposure we deserve. Right.
